title: AI agent built a complete tower defense in Godot, placed every tile, wrote every script, even found its own sound effects
author: jf_nash
selftext:
gave an ai agent some 3d tower defense assets and one prompt. it built the whole game through the godot editor without me touching anything

map with path tiles and spawn points, 4 tower types with different ranges and damage, enemy waves with scaling difficulty, gold economy, upgrade system, projectiles with particles, health bars, game over screen

then i told it to add sound effects. it searched for free audio online, downloaded the files, and hooked them up to the right game events on its own. tower firing sounds, enemy death sounds, wave announcements, ui feedback

this isnt code generation. the agent literally controls the editor, places nodes, sets properties, runs the game, finds errors, fixes them. like having a developer working inside godot

works with any mcp client. claude code cursor windsurf doesnt matter

[godotiq.com](http://godotiq.com)

replies.author: jf_nash
replies.body:
You’re absolutely right, we’re still in the early stages. I’m trying to promote it and see what people think, but few are giving feedback; a few have bought it anyway. What I can say is that the demos you see are genuine: no cherry-picking, no manual post-processing.

As for your 25 maps, it depends on the complexity. If they’re tile-based layouts (like the tower defence map in the video), the agent is perfectly capable of creating them quickly using the grid and scatter placement tools. You give it the tile assets and describe the layout you want, and it builds it in the editor with correct collisions and navigation.

The free version already includes scene creation tools, so you could literally try it out on a map and see if it works for your project before spending a penny. Perhaps make sure you run it in a separate directory to avoid any initial issues and to see if it’s right for you; in any case, I’d be really curious to know how it performs in your specific context.

replies.author: jf_nash
replies.body:
sure, the basic editor operations (place nodes, run game, read errors),yeah, most godot mcps do that. the free tier covers that too.
the paid part is the analysis layer that no other godot mcp has, spatial mapping that tells the agent where every object is and finds valid placement positions, dependency graphs, signal flow tracing across files, impact prediction before you change something. thats the stuff that stops the agent from putting objects inside walls or breaking 5 systems when it edits a signal.
if raw editor control is all you need, the free tier works fine for that. the pro is for when you want the agent to actually understand your project, not just execute commands in it.

comments.author: count023
comments.body: how did you integrate the whold godot ai pipeline exactly? you mention the godot editor, was this coworker or something?

replies.author: jf_nash
replies.body:
no colleagues, solo project. the integration is pretty straightforward actually

there's a small gdscript addon (4 files, \~500 lines) that runs inside the godot editor as a plugin. when you enable it, it starts a websocket server on localhost. thats the bridge

then there's a python mcp server that connects to that websocket. when an ai agent calls a tool like "place this node here" or "run the game", the python server sends the command over websocket to the addon, and the addon executes it through godot's own editor api. so the agent is using the same api a human developer uses when clicking around in the editor

the mcp part is just the protocol that lets any ai client (claude code, cursor, windsurf) talk to the python server in a standard way

so the pipeline is: ai agent → mcp protocol → python server → websocket → gdscript addon → godot editor api

no custom engine, no fork, no modifications to godot itself. just a plugin that gives the ai a way in

comments.author: ZuffaZombie
comments.body: How does this compare to godot mcp pro?

replies.author: jf_nash
replies.body:
different focus. godot mcp pro has 162 tools, mostly individual editor operations. add mesh, set material, create particle, configure physics body, etc. lots of granular control over the editor

godotiq has 36 tools but adds an intelligence layer on top. spatial analysis that tells the agent where every object is in 3d space, dependency graphs that show what breaks if you change something, signal flow tracing across files, smart placement that checks collisions and navmesh before placing objects

so godot mcp pro gives the agent more buttons to press. godotiq gives the agent understanding of what its doing. different tradeoffs it depends on whether you need breadth of operations or depth of analysis

both use websocket to talk to the editor, both work with any mcp client

comments.body:
Oh wow... I wanted to go Godot from Unity but Claude advised me not to because it said it can code worlds better in Unity due to the large training data set and existing, massive body of examples (which will change for Godot over time for sure)... You think it may have been off there?

I'd love to switch to Godot if my prompts don't start suddenly regressing to only half doing what I want.

Thanks to any for any input!!!<3

replies.author: jf_nash
replies.body:
claude's not wrong that there's more unity training data out there right now. but the gap is closing fast, and honestly the bigger issue isn't the model's knowledge, it's whether the agent can actually interact with the engine.

an ai can write you a perfect unity c# script but it still can't open the editor, place objects, run the game, or check if things work. you're still copy-pasting code and going back and forth.

with godot + an mcp server the agent literally controls the editor. places nodes, writes scripts, runs the game, checks errors, fixes stuff. the workflow is completely different from "generate code and hope it works"

i'm biased obviously (i built godotiq which does exactly this) but the point stands for any godot mcp setup. the training data gap matters less when the agent can see what it's doing and fix its own mistakes in real time

if you want to test it before committing to the switch, install godot and try the free tier of any godot mcp. you'll see pretty quick if the agent can handle what you need
